slides.title: Angle Pairs: Supplementary, Complementary, Vertical, Adjacent
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: four names for pairs of angles, and what each name tells you about their sizes.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is today's 'supplementary' before it has a name: a straight angle is 180°, so the other is 50°. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the names and the picture.
slides.note:
Two lines cross and make four angles. Angles 1 and 2 are adjacent: one vertex, one shared side, no overlap. Angles 1 and 3 are vertical: across the crossing — and equal (each makes a straight line with angle 2, so both are 180 minus the same angle). Angles 2 and 4 are vertical too.
OFF: 'Next to, sharing a side: adjacent. Across: vertical, and equal.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Complementary angles make 90° — a corner; supplementary angles make 180° — a straight line. A linear pair (adjacent, on a straight line) is supplementary: 60° and 120°. A square corner mark is a 90 nobody printed. The state's named mistake is swapping the two: complementary is the Corner, supplementary the Straight line.
OFF: 'Complementary: corner, 90. Supplementary: straight, 180.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
With expressions, the name gives the equation: a linear pair sums to 180, so 2x + 10 + 50 = 180, 2x = 120, x = 60 — and the angle is 2(60) + 10 = 130°, not 60. Vertical angles are equal: 3x − 5 = 70, x = 25. The book names 'reported x as the angle' three times: read what the question asks.
OFF: 'Name it, write it, solve it, put x back.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask what the square mark says before anyone writes: the two angles make 90 — complementary.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Complementary: 3x − 1 + 2x + 6 = 90, so 5x + 5 = 90, x = 17. Put it back: 3(17) − 1 = 50° and 2(17) + 6 = 40°; check 50 + 40 = 90. A board with 17 stopped at x.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 4x + x + 10 = 90, 5x = 80, x = 16: 64° and 26°. A board with 16 stopped at x; one with 34 used 180.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask what vertical angles do: they are equal — so the two expressions are set equal, variables on both sides (Unit 1).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Vertical, so equal: 5x − 12 = 2x + 18, 3x = 30, x = 10. Each angle is 5(10) − 12 = 38°, and 2(10) + 18 = 38° checks it. A board with 10 reported x; one with 180 added them as if supplementary.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 4x + 3 = x + 39, 3x = 36, x = 12: each angle 51°. A board with 12 reported x.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: 90 − 34 = 56°. A board with 146 used 180 — supplementary.

slides.note: a is across the crossing from 47°: vertical, so 47°. b is next to it on a straight line: 180 − 47 = 133°. (The 43-minute cut drops this board.)

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option A is the state's named swap, option C treats the pair as vertical, option D added. Split? Sixty seconds, convince your neighbour, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Supplementary: 3x + 120 = 180, 3x = 60, x = 20 (and the angle is 75°). A board with 30 set 3x + 15 = 105 — a linear pair is not equal.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Equal: 6x − 20 = 2x + 28, 4x = 48, x = 12, so each angle is 52°. A board with 12 reported x — the question asks for the angle.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9

slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the 50° below the line is bait. 38° and x° make the straight line above it: x = 142.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: two facts put together — equal, and adding to 90.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.

slides.note: IXL: every listed skill is required, SmartScore 67. Due at the start of the next class.
